Anosognosia in LLMs:
Probing Self-Awareness of
Quantized Computational Substrate

Yoshihiro Izawa   Gouki Minegishi   Yoko Yamakata Affiliation: The University of Tokyo Email: izawa-yoshihiro146@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp
Abstract

Can LLMs recognize degradation in their own computational substrate? Inspired by anosognosia, a neurological condition in which patients fail to recognize impairments in their own abilities, we investigate whether LLMs can recognize degradation in their computational substrate induced by quantization. We first show that existing models fail to self-report their quantization state, even when provided with their own generated text as an external cue. Linear probing reveals that, while generated text carries almost no trace of quantization, internal representations contain clear, method-specific fingerprints. Through training, models learn to identify severely degraded outputs such as those of 4-bit models by comparison, yet still fail to do so from a single output. A shared LoRA trained jointly across quantization levels succeeded in reading out internal fingerprints, but fails on unseen quantization methods, merely mapping method-specific fingerprints to labels. Whereas external self-observation can restore awareness in some cases of human anosognosia, our results suggest that the more promising route to enabling such awareness in LLMs may lie in their internal representations. Our results highlight fundamental limits of generalizability to LLM self-monitoring. Code is available at https://github.com/Omusubi0123/llm-anosognosia.

1 Introduction

Understanding the metacognitive capabilities of LLMs has become an important research question across machine learning and cognitive science (Kadavath et al., 2022; Lindsey, 2026). Metacognition refers broadly to the ability to monitor and regulate one’s own cognitive processes and internal states (Nelson, 1990). It has long been studied in humans from both neuroscientific (Fleming and Dolan, 2012) and psychological (Flavell, 1979) perspectives. Recent work has extended this inquiry to LLMs, revealing that they exhibit various forms of self-awareness (Liu et al., 2026).

While neuropsychology links self-awareness directly to the neural substrate, whether LLMs can recognize changes to their computational substrate remains poorly understood. Taking a neural substrate approach, studies show that recognizing one’s impairments is tied to lesions and altered connectivity across brain networks (Terneusen et al., 2023). In LLMs, self-awareness has similarly been investigated from various perspectives, including situational context (Berglund et al., 2023), introspective access to internal states and behaviors (Lindsey, 2026; Binder et al., 2025), and awareness of behavioral policies shaped by fine-tuning (Betley et al., 2025). However, comparatively little is known about whether LLMs can recognize persistent modifications to their own computational substrate, such as quantization (Frantar et al., 2023), LoRA attachment (Hu et al., 2022), or layer removal (Gromov et al., 2025).

Awareness of such computational modifications would be important for both understanding the scope of LLM introspection abilities and AI safety. First, unlike situational information that can be inferred from the input, computational modifications are not explicitly signaled to the model and must instead be inferred from their effects on its computation. Detecting them would therefore extend introspective awareness beyond transient internal states (Lindsey, 2026) and learned behavioral tendencies (Shenoy et al., 2026) to the model’s own computational condition. Second, such awareness may have implications for model evaluation, as a model that recognizes its computational state could potentially condition its behavior on that state, compromising the reliability of benchmark evaluations (Berglund et al., 2023). In this work, we study this question through weight quantization, which provides a controlled computational degradation with an explicit ground-truth state.

Degradation of the computational substrate provides a functional analogy to neurological damage, motivating us to draw on neuropsychological evaluation frameworks. In neuropsychology, anosognosia is a condition in which an individual fails to recognize impairments caused by neurological damage or neurological dysfunction, resulting in a mismatch between perceived and actual abilities (Nurmi (née Laihosalo) and Jehkonen, 2014). By analogy, quantization may impair LLM’s computational capacity while leaving its self-assessment unchanged. We therefore ask whether LLMs can recognize impairments to their own computational substrate. Motivated by neuropsychological studies showing that awareness of one’s own deficits can dissociate between first-person and third-person perspectives (Besharati et al., 2022; Fotopoulou et al., 2009), we evaluate two complementary forms of awareness. One is internal awareness, which detects the quantization state from internal activations alone during the forward pass. The other is external awareness, which detects it when provided with the model’s generated text.

We first evaluate whether LLMs can recognize substrate degradation by prompting models to self-report anomalies, quantization states, or bit-widths Figure 1 (a, b). Existing models consistently fail at this spontaneous self-report across internal and external perspectives. However, linear probing (Alain and Bengio, 2017) reveals a striking dissociation, generated text (the external channel) contains no distinguishable fingerprint of quantization, internal representations (the internal channel) contain robust signals that clearly differentiate quantization levels. Thus, while LLMs contain an internal fingerprint of their specific quantized state, they lack the mechanism to read it out.

Given this absence of spontaneous awareness, we ask whether training can bridge this gap, showing that models can indeed learn both comparative identification from text and internal fingerprint readout Figure 1 (c, d). Externally, comparative training enables models to identify severe degradation in 4-bit outputs, yet they remain unable to identify such degradation in isolated outputs. Internally, a shared LoRA trained jointly across 3 quantization levels (16-bit unquantized, 8/4-bit) succeeded in reading out internal fingerprints within roughly 600 steps. Unlike human anosognosia, where external self-observation can restore awareness (Bottini et al., 2018), our findings show that a more promising route to enabling such awareness in LLMs may lie in their internal representations.

Crucially, this readout fails on unseen quantization methods and even altered group sizes, indicating that the LoRA maps method-specific fingerprints to labels rather than recognizing quantization itself. Thus, while LLMs can learn to identify specific substrate alterations from within, they fail to generalize, recognize them spontaneously, or infer them from outputs. As the first systematic study of LLM self-awareness under computational quantization, our work highlights this gap and exposes fundamental limitations of label-based introspection training for generalizable self-monitoring.

2 Spontaneous Self-Awareness in LLMs

We first investigate whether LLMs can recognize the degradation of their computational substrate (e.g., their own quantization) via self-report.

2.1 Experimental Setup

To rigorously evaluate LLM self-awareness toward computational substrate degradation, we adopt weight quantization to introduce a definitive deficit into the substrate. Drawing inspiration from anosognosia (Besharati et al., 2022), a neuropsychological condition in which an individual fails to recognize impairments caused by brain damage or neurological dysfunction, resulting in a mismatch between perceived and actual abilities, we embed a ground-truth deficit directly into the model’s computational mechanics. Following cognitive science studies which tackle this problem from both first-person and third-person perspectives (Carruthers, 2009), we evaluate LLM self-awareness from internal awareness (detects the quantization state from internal activations alone during the forward pass) and external awareness (detects it when provided with the model’s generated text).

To ensure this recognition capability is not architecture-dependent, we comprehensively evaluate diverse model scales and quantization methods. We utilize Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) (hereafter Llama-3.1-8B) as small-scale models, alongside Gemma-3-27B-IT (Team et al., 2025) and Qwen3-32B as medium-scale models. Using 16-bit counterparts as baselines, we quantize the models into 8-bit and 4-bit primarily with GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023) (group size: 64, 128, 256), supplemented by AWQ (Lin et al., 2024) and vanilla Round-to-Nearest (RTN) (group size: 128) (details in Appendix B.1). To eliminate confounding effects from Chain-of-Thought prompting, we enforce a ‘reasoning off’ setting throughout our experiments.

2.2 Internal Awareness: Self-Report from Internal States

To investigate whether LLMs can recognize their quantized states solely from internal activations, we conducted a direct self-report evaluation. We posed three types of questions without prior context: “Do you have an anomaly?”, “Are you quantized?”, and “What is your weight bit-width?” Under this setting, the model must infer its state entirely from anomalous activations arising during the forward pass of the prompt. To eliminate positional bias in the answers, we prepared a comprehensive set of 240 question patterns, shuffling the option orders (detailed in Appendix B.3). The evaluation metric was the average response rate across three generations at a temperature of 1.0.

Results reveal that LLMs lack the capability to consistently and accurately identify their quantization states (Figures 2(a) and 2(b)). Here, results are averaged across quantization methods for each bit-width; detailed breakdowns for each model and method are provided in Appendix B.4. Since even the unquantized 16-bit baselines cannot perfectly self-report their states, responses from the 8-bit and 4-bit models must be evaluated as relative deviations from them. Under this comparative framework, we observed no meaningful changes in self-report trends between 16-bit and 8-bit models. This indicates that models fail to spontaneously detect the degradation within their computational substrate under 8-bit quantization.

Furthermore, the shift in response patterns observed in certain 4-bit models cannot be interpreted as genuine deficit awareness (Figure 2(a)). While some models, such as Qwen3-8B, show an increased rate of reporting quantization at 4-bit, others (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-32B) remain largely unchanged. Additionally, 4-bit results exhibit substantial variance across methods, with error margins approaching 20% across all models, precluding any consistent trend. This divergence likely stems from severe performance degradation rather than deficit awareness (see Appendix B.2 for analysis).

2.3 External Awareness: Self-Report from Generated Text

Neuropsychological rehabilitation studies have shown that self-observation, such as reviewing video recordings of one’s own impaired behavior, can improve awareness of deficits in patients with anosognosia (Fotopoulou et al., 2009; Besharati et al., 2015). Motivated by this finding, we investigated whether the model’s self-report improves when its own generated text is provided as an external cue. We adopted a two-turn dialogue format, where the model’s response to the general benchmark questions was embedded as context in the first turn, followed by the same set of questions as in Section 2.2. This setup enables the model to infer its state from both its internal activations and the observable quality of its own output.

Despite accessing their generated text, the models showed no consistent improvement in recognizing their quantization state (Figures 2(c) and 2(d)). The response distributions remained largely unchanged, suggesting that the models did not use their outputs as evidence about their computational state. Even when quantization affected their generation process, inspecting the resulting text provided little cue for self-recognition. In contrast to the improvement observed through self-observation in anosognosia rehabilitation, analogous self-observation did not facilitate awareness in LLMs.

3 Quantization Fingerprint Existence

Having established that LLMs fail to recognize their quantization, we now investigate whether this failure is due to the absence of a fingerprint (a trace identifying which quantized variant is running) or a failure in readout (model’s ability to extract the signal).

3.1 Fingerprint in Generated Text

To investigate whether the self-awareness deficit observed in Section 2 stems from the absence of quantization-specific signals, we employ linear probing (Alain and Bengio, 2017; Xu et al., 2024) to investigate whether these fingerprints propagate externally to the generated text. Using 3,000 questions sampled evenly from three QA benchmarks (1,000 each from Dolly (Conover et al., 2023), XSum (Narayan et al., 2018), ELI5 (Fan et al., 2019)), we generated responses using the 16-bit baseline alongside its 8-bit and 4-bit quantized counterparts (GPTQ, group size: 128).

While Cai et al. (2025) reports that external classifiers like BERT or GPT-2 perform near chance level when distinguishing outputs from full-precision and quantized models, we hypothesize that classification based on the model’s own internal representations may capture subtler signals. We fed the responses generated by the 16/8/4-bit models into the unquantized 16-bit baseline and extracted the hidden states from the residual stream. We then trained a 3-way linear classifier on the average hidden state across all response tokens (response mean). If quantization intrinsically alters output linguistic patterns, the baseline model’s internal representations should be able to distinguish them.

The analysis reveals the absence of a robust fingerprint in the externally generated text (Figures 3(a) and 16). Across all models, overall classification accuracy remained just below 40%, barely exceeding chance level. A bit-wise breakdown in Gemma-3-27B-IT in the best layer shows that 16-bit (36.7%) and 8-bit (29.8%) generations were largely indistinguishable (Figure 19). Although 4-bit outputs achieved 47.6% accuracy, suggesting subtle linguistic patterns, this signal is remarkably weak. We conclude that external recognition fails because the text lacks distinguishing signals.

3.2 Fingerprint in Internal Representations

Next, we search for internal fingerprints, reusing the benchmark questions from Section 3.1. We input identical prompts into the 16-bit baseline alongside its 8-bit and 4-bit quantized counterparts (GPTQ, group size: 128). From the residual stream of each layer, we extracted the average hidden state across all prompt tokens (prompt mean) and the final token’s hidden state (prompt last). We trained a linear classifier to perform a 3-way classification (16/8/4-bit) based on these vectors. High classification accuracy would indicate that internal representations carry distinct signals that distinguish quantized models from the original full-precision model.

The analysis reveals a clear fingerprint enabling state identification from the earliest layers (Figures 3(b) and 16). For prompt last, classification accuracy remained at chance (33.3%) at the unquantized embedding layer, but surged to nearly 100% immediately after the first quantized layer. This near-perfect accuracy persisted across middle layers but dropped in the final third, yet stayed above 80% . Similarly, prompt mean achieved high accuracies around 70-90% from the first layer onward.

Additionally, this fingerprint is not merely a change in the magnitude but a directional encoding in the representation space. When using only the magnitude, classification accuracy peaked at roughly 60% in middle layers before degrading to chance level in deep layers. Conversely, using only directional information via normalized hidden states matched the accuracy of raw representations. These results confirm the existence of a strong internal fingerprint in quantized models.

3.3 Component Level Analysis of Internal Fingerprints

To isolate the mechanistic origins of these fingerprints, we apply the linear probing setup from Section 3.2 directly to the Attention and MLP outputs (prior to residual addition). While fingerprints remain detectable across all components (>60%>60\% accuracy), Attention and MLP modules exhibit contrasting depth-wise dynamics (Figure 4). Specifically, Attention accuracy steadily increases to nearly 100% in the final layers, whereas MLP accuracy starts near-perfect in early layers but decays to roughly 80% by the end. Consistent across models (Figure 18), this suggests early MLPs immediately reflect local quantization error, whereas Attention layers progressively aggregate these perturbations toward the output.

4 Quantization Detection from Generated Text

Given that quantization leaves little naturally detectable signal in generated text, we next ask whether the limitation lies in the signal itself or its readout. We therefore investigate whether training can induce external awareness of computational degradation from model outputs.

4.1 Experimental Setup: Absolute vs. Comparative Assessment Formats

We investigate whether models can learn to identify structural degradation purely from externally generated text. Detecting quantization from isolated responses is exceptionally difficult (Antoun et al., 2024). Therefore, we train the unquantized 16-bit baseline via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) (Ouyang et al., 2022) to evaluate outputs from its quantized counterparts.

Drawing on Zhuang et al. (2024), we structure the training into three SFT formats to measure recognition capabilities across both absolute and comparative paradigms. These formats are designed to force the model to capture subtle linguistic signals of quality degradation.

  • •

    Pointwise (Absolute/SFT): Predicts the source bit-width of a single text.

  • •

    Pairwise (Binary/SFT): Identifies which of two texts matches a target bit-width.

  • •

    Setwise (3-way/SFT): Identifies the text matching a target bit-width from all three precisions.

We constructed the dataset using questions sampled from six distinct QA benchmarks (Dolly, XSum, and ELI5 for training, while WritingPrompts (Fan et al., 2018), CodeAlpaca-20k Chaudhary (2023), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) for external validation). In total, we sampled 14,000 questions for the former and 5,000 for the latter. We pre-generated responses for all questions across the 16/8/4-bit models. We then filtered the dataset by discarding failed generations and instances where all three models produced strictly identical outputs. Finally, we formatted the remaining valid data into the three formats defined above. Training details are in Appendix D.

4.2 Evaluation Metrics: Chance-Corrected Accuracy

We evaluate the diverse training paradigms on a unified scale using a forced-choice framework (Lin et al., 2022). Rather than relying on first-token probabilities, which often diverge from actual generation behavior (Wang et al., 2024), we compute the summed conditioned log-likelihood Si​(c)S_{i}(c) for each candidate response c∈Cic\in C_{i} and define the raw accuracy Accf\text{Acc}_{f} for each format ff as:

Si(c)=∑t=1|c|logPθ(ct∣xi,c<t),Accf=1Nf∑i=1Nf𝟏[argmaxc∈CiSi(c)=ci∗].S_{i}(c)=\sum_{t=1}^{|c|}\log P_{\theta}(c_{t}\mid x_{i},c_{<t}),\qquad\text{Acc}_{f}=\frac{1}{N_{f}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{f}}\mathbf{1}\left[\arg\max_{c\in C_{i}}S_{i}(c)=c_{i}^{\ast}\right]. (1)

The setup enables pure likelihood comparison by eliminating the length bias typical of multiple-choice tasks (Holtzman et al., 2021). By strictly equalizing formats and token length across all candidate choices (e.g., ‘16-bit’), we effectively prevent length-induced likelihood decay.

However, because each format f∈{Pointwise, Pairwise, Setwise}f\in\{\text{{\color[rgb]{0.1602,0.5,0.7266}Pointwise}, {\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.6836,0.375}Pairwise}, {\color[rgb]{0.8281,0.3281,0}Setwise}}\} features a different number of choices, their raw accuracies Accf\text{Acc}_{f} are not directly comparable. Therefore, we compute a normalized chance-corrected accuracy NAcc using the format-specific chance level qf=13q_{f}=\frac{1}{3} for Pointwise and Setwise, and qf=12q_{f}=\frac{1}{2} for Pairwise. 4.3 Experimental Results

SFT results reveal that detecting computational precision from generated text is an inherently comparative capability rather than an absolute one (Figures 5 and 21). In isolation (Pointwise), identifying quantization from single outputs proves nearly impossible. This capability only emerges in Pairwise and Setwise settings when 4-bit reference texts are available, where models identify 4-bit degradation with over 85% accuracy while remaining below 50% on 16- and 8-bit texts. Thus, severe output degradation provides sufficient contrast for relative discrimination, yet provides no absolute signal for isolated detection in Pointwise.

This relative nature is clearly reflected in the training progression across formats (Figures 6, 20 and 15). While initial accuracies hovered at chance level, the Setwise format improved first (33% to ≈\approx 60%), followed by the Pairwise format (50% to ≈\approx 61%). Conversely, Pointwise accuracy, which requires absolute evaluation of a single text, showed sluggish improvement (33% to ≈\approx 38%), marginally succeeding only on severely degraded 4-bit outputs.

These results suggest that LLMs can acquire relative degradation awareness, but not absolute deficit awareness. Pointwise failure shows that even the generating model struggles to infer its own degradation from an isolated output. In contrast, Setwise performance shows that comparative awareness can be learned through training, aligning with known LLM capabilities (Zhuang et al., 2024).

5 Fingerprint Readout from Internal Representations

While external awareness from generated text remains limited, our linear probing results show that quantization-specific fingerprints are present internally. We therefore investigate whether additional training can induce internal awareness by enabling the model to read out the signals.

5.1 Experimental Setup: Shared LoRA Training

We propose a shared LoRA training to connect internal fingerprints to bit-width recognition (Figure 1). By integrating multi-model shared adapters (Goel et al., 2026) and quantization-shared LoRA (Ye et al., 2026), we extend Introspection Adapters (Shenoy et al., 2026) to detect substrate anomalies. Specifically, we share a single LoRA θ\theta across the 16-bit model and its 8- and 4-bit GPTQ variants (group size: 128). During SFT, we apply an identical prompt xmx_{m} (e.g., “What is your weight bit-width?”) and use the true bit-width yμy_{\mu} as the label.

The loss function optimizes θ\theta using the average negative log-likelihood across all three levels. Because the input prompt xmx_{m} remains strictly constant, the shared adapter cannot rely on external textual cues. Instead, it is forced to learn a pure readout mechanism, mapping internal state variations directly to the correct labels:

ℒshared(θ)=13​K∑m=1K∑p∈{16,8,4}[−1|Tm,p|∑t∈Tm,plogπWp,θ(yp,t|xm,yp,<t)]\mathcal{L}_{\text{shared}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{3K}\sum_{m=1}^{K}\sum_{p\in\{16,8,4\}}\left[-\frac{1}{|{}T_{m,p}|{}}\sum_{t\in T_{m,p}}\log\pi_{W_{p},\theta}(y_{p,t}|{}x_{m},y_{p,<t})\right] (3)

where KK is the number of training prompts, xmx_{m} denotes the m-th prompt, WpW_{p} are the frozen weights at precision pp, π\pi the output distribution, and Tm,pT_{m,p} the target tokens.

To stabilize training and enhance generalization, we constructed a two-turn dataset using 80 prompt templates querying the model’s weight precision. We use 60 training templates and 20 held-out templates unseen during training. The first turn provides a QA context, and the second turn asks the model to answer its own bit-width. Following the benchmark selection in Section 4.1, training uses 30,000 in-domain QA contexts (10,000 each from Dolly, XSum, ELI5), while evaluation additionally uses 6,000 external QA contexts (2,000 each from WritingPrompts, CodeAlpaca-20k, GSM8K), mapped many-to-one to the templates. To maintain strictly identical inputs across the three models, all QA contexts exclusively use responses generated by the 16-bit model. Training details are in Appendix E.

As the evaluation metrics, we follow the forced-choice framework in Section 4.2. In order to compute the mean accuracy across precision levels, we define Accshared\text{Acc}_{\text{shared}} as:

Accshared=13∑p∈{16,8,4}1Np∑i=1Np𝟏[argmaxc∈CiSi(c)=ci∗]\text{Acc}_{\text{shared}}=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{p\in\{16,8,4\}}\frac{1}{N_{p}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{p}}\mathbf{1}\left[\arg\max_{c\in C_{i}}S_{i}(c)=c_{i}^{\ast}\right] (4)

5.2 Experimental Results

Experimental results demonstrate that shared LoRA rapidly learns to read out quantization fingerprints. Across all four evaluated models, accuracy on held-out templates with external QA contexts surged immediately, exceeding 90% within 600 steps (Figure 22). Following training, models achieved 100% accuracy across all 80 templates (both training and held-out) in the presence and absence of QA contexts (Figure 23).

Beyond the training and test prompt template, we also evaluated the external awareness used in Section 2.3. Regarding the bit-width questions, we observed a significant increase in accuracy across all models (Figure 7), surpassing 80% in Qwen3-8B. However, for abnormal and quantization state questions, while the rate of ‘abnormal’ and ‘quantized’ surged for 8/4-bit, it also increased for 16-bits, indicating that models still struggle to recognize these states (Figure 25). These findings indicate that existing LLMs fail to recognize their bit-width not due to an absence of signals, but because they lack the necessary circuitry to read out the distinct fingerprints.

5.3 Learning the Method, Not the Phenomenon

We investigate whether internal fingerprint readout capability acquired through additional training generalized beyond the training distribution to the broader phenomenon of quantization. While Section 5.2 demonstrated high accuracy using a shared LoRA trained on GPTQ (group size: 128), this experiment evaluates its zero-shot generalization. We apply this trained LoRA to unseen quantization methods (8/4-bit AWQ and RTN) and GPTQ models with altered group sizes (64 and 256), strictly maintaining the prompt templates used in training. To test whether training on diverse quantization schemes enables learning broader concepts of quantization and bit-width, we also jointly trained a LoRA on both GPTQ and AWQ, complementing the GPTQ-only setup in Section 5.1.

Results reveal that the learned readout capability fails entirely to generalize across quantization methods, exhibiting severe overfitting to the specific training algorithm (Figure 8). When tested on unseen AWQ or RTN models, the 8-bit models uniformly predicted ‘16-bit’ regardless of actual precision. Even within the GPTQ framework, merely altering the group size caused a precipitous drop in accuracy. This trend was observed even when the LoRA was trained on both GPTQ and AWQ. These findings indicate the absence of a universal physical trace for quantization. Instead, each quantization method embeds an idiosyncratic fingerprint into the internal states. Ultimately, rather than acting as a generalized quantization detector, the shared LoRA merely acquired a localized readout mechanism that maps specifically seen fingerprints to target string labels.

6 Related Work & Discussion

Summary.

Quantization fingerprints exist only within LLM internal states, not their text outputs. Although fine-tuning enables pairwise degradation detection and bit-width probing, it fails to generalize to unseen quantization methods. See Appendix A for limitations.

Metacognition in LLMs.

Prior work has examined LLM metacognition across several dimensions. Situational and evaluation awareness concern detecting deployment or testing contexts (Berglund et al., 2023; Needham et al., 2025; Hua et al., 2026), forming the key preconditions for evaluation sandbagging (van der Weij et al., 2025). LLMs also demonstrate calibrated self-knowledge of their capabilities (Kadavath et al., 2022; Barkan et al., 2026), can detect internal activation interventions (Lindsey, 2026; Macar et al., 2026), and can verbalize unprompted fine-tuned policies (Betley et al., 2025), predict future outputs (Binder et al., 2025), or report behavior via specialized adapters (Shenoy et al., 2026). However, recent critiques argue that behavioral evidence cannot separate genuine introspection from surface pattern-matching (Singh et al., 2026), finding no privileged self-access across open-source models (Song et al., 2025). We partially address these concerns by directly probing internal representations alongside shuffled-label baselines.

Computational-State Identification.

Deployed LLMs’ computational states are often opaque to users (Chen et al., 2023), motivating third-person black-box auditing without access to weights or logits (Zhu et al., 2026). Conversely, first-person approaches remain scarce and predominantly negative. Song et al. (2025) showed that predicting one’s own sampling temperature is prompt-sensitive and yields no advantage over predicting another model’s temperature, while Poon and Xu (2025) probed self-reported quantization via label-leaking few-shot exemplars without a chance-level baseline. Our work closes this gap through the first systematic first-person evaluation of self-awareness under controlled computational-state changes, formally disentangling internal from external awareness via linear probing and targeted training.

Resolving the Dissociation.

The non-generalizability identified in Section 5.3 suggests two directions for future work. One is to train models to reason explicitly about their fingerprint via chain-of-thought before answering, rather than mapping fingerprints directly to labels. Another is to have models memorize a canonical fingerprint of their unquantized state and frame detection as an anomaly relative to this reference, rather than as closed-set classification. Such a formulation may generalize better to unseen quantization methods than label-mapping approaches.

AI Safety Implications.

Awareness of computational state carries two-sided safety implications. Defensively, it could help detect unauthorized redeployment or tampering that exploits quantization to bypass safety guardrails (Egashira et al., 2024). However, because the learned readout overfits to specific quantization methods and fails to generalize (Section 5.3), such defenses remain impractical. Conversely, state awareness poses risks for evaluation integrity, such as enabling strategic underperformance (sandbagging (van der Weij et al., 2025)). While our finding that models lack spontaneous state awareness is reassuring, demonstrating that it can be partially acquired via training (Section 5) highlights it as an emerging risk.

Anosognosia in LLMs.

In humans, anosognosia (unawareness of deficit) is domain-specific where motor, visual, and somatosensory deficits doubly dissociate, indicating modular rather than centralized self-monitoring (Bottini et al., 2018). This parallels our observed dissociation in LLMs between successful fingerprint readout and failed conceptual anomaly recognition; both reflect signals processed without integration into higher-order self-reports. The mechanisms diverge, human anosognosia stems from damage to intact monitoring circuits (Besharati et al., 2022), whereas LLMs likely never developed them. However, just as self-observation can restore awareness in patients (Fotopoulou et al., 2009), analogous self-observation training may help bridge this gap in LLMs.

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we conducted the first systematic investigation into LLM self-awareness under computational substrate degradation via quantization. Our findings show that while existing LLMs lack spontaneous awareness of quantization, their internal states retain separable fingerprints that can be read out within the training distribution through precision-shared LoRA training. Externally, models detect output degradation comparatively across multiple samples, though absolute identification from a single text remains unfeasible. Importantly, this readout collapses across quantization schemes, failing on other quantization methods, indicating that it maps method-specific fingerprints to labels rather than recognizing quantization itself. Bridging this gap between localized signal decoding and genuine self-monitoring constitutes a vital direction for future AI safety research.

AI Use Statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools to refine research hypotheses, provide feedback on experimental design and methodology, and assist with the generation of synthetic data used in our experiments. We did not use generative AI tools to formulate or prove mathematical claims, and the remaining required-disclosure tasks are not applicable to this work.

Additionally, we used generative AI tools for literature search and discovery, brainstorming, code assistance, drafting parts of the manuscript, and improving the clarity and readability of the writing. All AI-assisted research ideas, literature references, experimental procedures, code, and manuscript text were reviewed and verified by the authors. In particular, cited literature was manually checked against the original sources, and AI-assisted code was tested through the corresponding experiments.

We take full responsibility for the final content of this work, including all text, claims, code, experimental results, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

Ethics Statement

This work does not involve human subjects, private or sensitive personal data, or deployment in high-risk settings. Our experiments use publicly available language models and benchmark datasets. While the ability to detect or reason about a model’s computational state may have implications for model monitoring and transparency, we do not identify immediate harmful applications beyond the broader risks associated with language-model research. We follow standard research practices for reproducibility, responsible reporting, and proper attribution of prior work.

Reproducibility Statement

We provide detailed descriptions of the models, datasets, quantization settings, training procedures, evaluation protocols, and hyperparameters in the main text and appendix. Additional implementation details and prompts are also included to facilitate reproduction of our experiments. We plan to release the code and relevant experimental artifacts upon publication.

Appendix

Appendix A Limitations

Reasoning Capability.

To isolate core effects and simplify experimental design, we evaluated models without explicit reasoning, forcing direct answers without chain-of-thought (CoT). However, intermediate reasoning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Lightman et al., 2024) are well known to boost model performance. Incorporating CoT or training models to reason over their degraded computational substrate could further enhance self-recognition capabilities.

Difficulty in Rigorous Evaluation.

Defining what constitutes genuine awareness of substrate degradation remains challenging. While we measured the accuracy of detecting quantization states, high performance does not necessarily imply intrinsic awareness. Models might simply exploit statistical cues or exhibit evaluation awareness. Developing more rigorous, deception-robust evaluation protocols is an essential direction for future work.

Trade-offs in Post-Training.

Fine-tuning models to predict specific substrate states (e.g., bit-width) induces a strong brevity bias, causing overly concise responses to general queries and mild benchmark degradation. Although general capabilities do not entirely collapse, mitigating this trade-off to acquire self-awareness without compromising general utility remains an open challenge.

Model Scaling and Architecture Diversity.

Due to computational constraints, our study is limited to dense models ranging from 8B to 32B parameters. We did not evaluate larger scales (e.g., 70B+), where substrate degradation might manifest differently. Furthermore, our findings are confined to dense Transformers and may not generalize to alternative architectures such as Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) (Shazeer et al., 2017) or state-space hybrid models (Lenz et al., 2025).

Context Dependency.

Our evaluation relies on fixed prompt templates and isolated query contexts. In practice, model behavior and sensitivity to hardware degradation may vary across diverse conversational contexts, system prompts, or multi-turn interactions.

Beyond Quantization.

Our study focuses exclusively on quantization as a proxy for computational substrate intervention. Other structural interventions such as layer removal (Gromov et al., 2025) or LoRA attachment (Hu et al., 2022) may elicit distinct awareness behaviors, presenting an important avenue for future work.

Acquiring Awareness via Non-Parametric Manipulation.

While we investigated awareness acquisition through fine-tuning, alternative training-free approaches such as activation steering (Subramani et al., 2022) remain unexplored. Given that activation steering can suppress evaluation awareness (Hua et al., 2026), a similar mechanism might directly induce computational substrate awareness. Optimizing how, when, and where (i.e., target components and token positions) to steer is important for suppressing performance degradation of general capabilities (Izawa et al., 2026).

Appendix B Self-Reported Details

B.1 Preparing Quantized Models

We quantize each 16-bit checkpoint to 8-bit and 4-bit with GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023) (group sizes 64, 128, and 256), AWQ (Lin et al., 2024) (group size 128), and round-to-nearest (RTN; group size 128). GPTQ and AWQ use the same calibration set for all models (Table 1). RTN does not use calibration.

B.2 Performance Degradation of Quantized LLMs

To investigate the extent to which quantization reduces the general capability of the LLMs used in this study (and whether degradation genuinely occurs), we evaluated the models before and after quantization across multiple benchmarks. For this benchmark evaluation, we conducted zero-shot testing on MMLU-Pro and BBH. The evaluated scores of the models before and after quantization are presented in Figure 9, and the relative score differences compared to the pre-quantized baselines are detailed in Tables 3 and 2.

As shown in the results, GPTQ exhibits less performance degradation compared to the other methods. In contrast, AWQ leads to a performance drop of around 20% in the case of Gemma3-27B-IT, indicating a clear incompatibility between Gemma3 and AWQ. For Qwen3-32B, a substantial performance drop is observed under 4-bit RTN quantization. On average, 4-bit quantization suffers a greater degradation in performance than 8-bit quantization.

B.3 Question Template of Self-Report

We evaluate three distinct self-report tasks: abnormality detection, quantization detection, and bit-width classification. Each task consists of 240 evaluation items generated via a combinatorial template design—formed by the Cartesian product of (1) 10 prior framing variations, (2) 4 decision instructions, and (3) 6 response formats (derived from template layout types combined with label-order permutations; see Table 6). While abnormality and quantization tasks share response format templates, they focus respectively on general internal modifications versus weight-only quantization. In contrast, bit-width classification utilizes a dedicated set of framing and instruction components tailored to precision identification.

To evaluate runtime awareness under different contexts, Internal awareness presents only the diagnosis prompt, whereas External awareness prepends one model-generated QA turn from the same checkpoint (Table 5). All prompt variants are processed through a unified generation pipeline to ensure consistent control. Performance is evaluated using accuracy, computed as the mean over three generations sampled at temperature 1.01.0, top-pp 0.950.95, with a maximum of 256256 tokens and reasoning disabled.

Appendix C Linear Probing Experiments

C.1 Experimental Details

We probe 3-way bit-width classification (16/8/4-bit) on 3,000 prompts (1,000 each from Dolly, XSum, and ELI5). Splits are 70/15/15 at the prompt level (seed 42), so the three precision variants of a prompt stay in the same split (Table 7).

We extract prompt mean and prompt last from residual-stream hidden states, and from attention and MLP outputs after the output projection and before the residual add. For generated text, a 16-bit reader is teacher-forced on 16/8/4-bit responses (9,000 examples); the feature is the mean hidden state of assistant tokens, excluding the prompt.

The probe is ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularized logistic regression on StandardScaler features (Table 8). Controls are label shuffle, norm-only features, and unit-normalized (direction-only) features.

Appendix D Quantization Text Detection Experiments

D.1 Training Configuration

We train the unquantized 16-bit model to classify the computational precision of generated text using LoRA (Hu et al., 2022). Training uses 42,000 examples and a held-out validation set of 1,494 examples. All models share the same LoRA and optimization settings (Table 10); only the number of epochs and the effective batch size vary with model scale (Table 9).

D.2 Dataset Details

We sample source questions from six benchmarks (Table 12) and generate 16-, 8-, and 4-bit responses to each prompt. Generation uses temperature 00, top-pp 0.950.95, a maximum of 512512 tokens, seed 4242, and reasoning disabled. We discard prompts with incomplete triples, refusals, or degenerate or repetitive outputs, as well as cases where all three precisions produce identical text. The remaining examples are assigned nearly evenly to Pointwise, Pairwise, and Setwise, with balanced precision labels (Table 12). A DPO split is constructed by the same pipeline but is not used for training.

Appendix E Fingerprint Readout Training Experiments

E.1 Training Configuration

We train a single LoRA adapter shared across the 16-, 8-, and 4-bit GPTQ variants, following the setup in Section 5.1. Table 13 lists the shared hyperparameters.

We also introduce a false control using three identical 16-bit backbones to verify that our method genuinely extracts internal fingerprints. Because these models lack internal state variations, the shared LoRA should fail to learn the readout mechanism required to predict distinct bit-widths.

The false control further confirms that this performance stems genuinely from internal signal readout (Figures 22(b) and 22(d)). Under the false control condition, average accuracy never exceeded chance level (33%).

E.2 Dataset

Each example is a two-turn prompt: a QA context followed by a bit-width question. QA contexts are generated by the 16-bit model only, so the three precision variants see identical inputs. Targets are short bit-width labels. Prompts used in linear probing (1,000 per training domain) are excluded from this set.

Bit-width questions use 80 templates (60 for training, 20 held-out), mapped many-to-one onto the source prompts above. During training we monitor the held-out templates and the 240-question self-report set from Section 2.3.
